newsitem.title: FINLAND: Glaxo targets growth through smaller buys.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo targets growth through smaller buys.

text.p: More consolidation is ahead in pharmaceuticals but the industry is likely to remain fragmented, said the world's largest drugs company Glaxo Wellcome Plc on Tuesday, adding it will focus on smaller purchases.
New products should also offset lower sales of Glaxo's money-spinning anti-ulcer drug Zantac, which goes off patent in the United States and Britain this July, Glaxo said.

"As the business consolidates in the future, I think it will do so either by taking small pieces that will build the business, or doing it on a regional basis," chief executive Sir Richard Sykes told a news conference during an in-house visit.

"If we look forward, as far as we're concerned...we might have to acquire small businesses in a region or a country," he said. "We might have to acquire products that fit our portfolio and build our portfolio -- I would see those sorts of activities being much more common than big acquisitions."

Briefing journalists on future trends in global pharmaceuticals, Sykes said mega-mergers were becoming more difficult not least because of the cost, and noted that world leaders in drugs had no more than five percent market share.
He saw this continuing because the diversity of medical treatments was so immense.

Glaxo's overall five percent market share varied country-by-country, he said, adding that the challenge now is to build up a strong presence in developing markets which currently make up just 15 percent of sales.

"In some countries, like Japan which is the second largest pharmaceuticals country in the world, we have 1.8 (percent). That's not enough, because we should be aiming for at least five percent market share," he said.
"Now we will not get that by organic growth."

Asked about the impact of the end of the Zantac patent, Sykes said at end-1994 Zantac made up 40 percent of Glaxo's sales, which -- partly through its merger with Wellcome in 1995 -- had already fallen to 24 percent in the first half of 1996.
"We just happen to have the largest selling pharmaceutical product in the world coming off patent," Sykes said.

"It will be a difficult time because Zantac will do okay to the middle of the year...but we believe that through new product growth and product introductions that we can keep sales reasonably well intact during 1997," he said.

The main growth areas for Glaxo today were in AIDS, drugs for the central nervous system and drugs for respiratory problems, he said. "That's growing very rapidly. Asthma is becoming a very serious disease now all over the world."
But it was "nonsense" to think in terms of blockbuster drugs -- a broad portfolio in continuous development with a steady flow of new products was better longer-term.
Glaxo's own new products would boost the areas where it is strong and include a new departure in anti-diabetes products. "The new products are growing all the time," he said.

But when asked if his visit was linked to any plan to buy, for instance, Finnish drugs group Orion-yhtyma Oy, Sykes referred the question to the Finnish unit's managing director Jaakko Aalto, who said: "I have no such money."
